title: What the homepage has to prove for a law practice
metaTitle: What a law practice homepage must prove
excerpt: A law practice homepage should name the matters you take and offer a way to request a consultation. Marble and Latin do neither job.
alt: A clothing shop with racks, rope-hung industrial lamps, and a mirror, a specific room in the same way a homepage should name a specific matter.
caption: A shop that shows its racks, its lamps, and its mirror without a costume. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What does a law practice homepage need to show first?
faqs.answer: It needs to show the kind of matter the practice takes, and a way to request a consultation. A client who is choosing counsel under time pressure uses those two facts to decide whether to stay. A marble texture and a Latin motto do not answer either question.

faqs.question: Should a law firm homepage list every practice area?
faqs.answer: Lead with the matters you most want, and give each one a boundary. Link the rest from a services page. Twelve areas in equal type turn the homepage into a directory, and a hurried client cannot tell which work you actually stand behind.

faqs.question: Where should the consultation request sit?
faqs.answer: Put a labeled control in the first view on a phone, with one sentence about what the consultation is. Name, email, the kind of matter, and a deadline are enough for a first request. A long form before anyone replies gives a client with a real deadline a reason to leave.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A law practice homepage has one job when the reader is a client choosing counsel under time pressure. It names the kind of matter you take, and it offers a way to request a consultation. Nielsen Norman Group's 2011 review of page-visit research puts a clock on that job. People often leave a web page within 10 to 20 seconds, and the first 10 seconds are when they decide whether to stay.

Write those two facts in that order, in words the client already uses. A marble texture and a line of Latin do not name a matter, and they do not open a consultation. Google's guidance on helpful content gives extra weight to trust on topics that can affect a person's safety, health, or financial stability, the group it calls Your Money or Your Life. Choosing counsel sits in that group. The first screen has to earn the next minute with a specific offer.

## The two facts, in that order

The kind of matter comes first. A person holding a letter, a deadline, or a deal that closes on Friday does not have patience for a firm that might do everything. They need to know whether their problem is one you take.

Name the matters in ordinary words. "Commercial leases for independent shops." "Employment disputes for companies under fifty people." "Estate plans for a family with a house and a small business." Each line lets someone sort themselves in or out. A line about full-service counsel for discerning clients does not.

The consultation comes second, and it has to be visible in the same first view. The label should say what they are asking for. "Request a consultation" is a clear action. "Learn more" sends them to another page that still has to do this job. "Submit" tells them nothing about what happens next.

If you can say only one sentence above the action, use it for the matter. The year the firm opened, the city, and a line about care can sit nearby when they are true and short. They do not replace the matter or the request.

## What a matter line has to include

A useful matter line has three parts. The problem. The client. The boundary.

The problem is the thing they would tell a friend. A lease they do not understand. A co-founder dispute. A visa. A parent who died with a house and a bank account. Use that language on the first screen. Internal names such as practice group, contentious, and transactional can exist where a referring lawyer would look for them. They should not be the only words a client sees.

The client is who you are willing to sit with. A landlord. A tenant. An owner-led company with its first serious contract. If you act for both sides of a dispute, say so, and say that you run a conflict check before any advice. A hurried person would rather learn the limit now than after they have written their story into a form.

The boundary is the work you do not take. Personal injury. Criminal defense. Matters outside the jurisdictions where you are allowed to practice. A short no is a kindness. It saves the client a day, and it saves the firm an intake call that cannot go anywhere.

Lead with the matter the practice actually wants. Link the others. A homepage that gives twelve areas equal weight is a directory. A homepage that leads with the work you stand behind, and files the rest under a services link, is a practice with a point of view.

Jurisdiction belongs in that first cluster when the client needs a lawyer in a particular place. "We practice in Victoria" is a sorting fact. A skyline, or a marble field, is not. If you have two offices, name the cities and which matters each office takes. A single vague "serving clients nationwide" line makes a local client do the sorting you should have done.

## The consultation, placed where the glance lands

The request has to be a real control, with words, in the first view on a phone. A text link in the footer is a second chance. It is a poor primary offer.

Say what the consultation is, in one sentence beside the button. Twenty minutes to hear the deadline and to say whether you can help. A paid first meeting. A coordinator who reads the note the same weekday. Pick the version that is true. A client under time pressure is also judging whether you will waste the hour they do not have.

Keep the first step short. Ask for the kind of matter, a deadline if there is one, and a way to reply. Name, email, and one sentence are enough to request time. The opposing party's name, which you may need before you can speak freely, can be the second question. It should not be buried in a form of ten fields. A long form before any human reply feels like a test. People with a hearing date will go to the next firm that lets them ask.

State what the first reply will not do. It will not give legal advice. It will say whether the matter is one you take, and how the conversation gets booked. That sentence keeps an auto-reply from being mistaken for counsel.

## Why marble and Latin fail this buyer

Marble, columns, a scale, and a Latin motto are a costume many partners already trust. The costume reassures the people inside the firm that the site looks like a law practice. It does not tell a client whether you review commercial leases.

Latin fails for a practical reason. The client is reading fast, often on a phone, often anxious. A sentence they cannot translate did not help them sort the matter. If a motto matters to the firm, put the English beside it on the about page, after the work is clear.

Stock marble also flattens the practice into every other firm that bought the same texture. The client cannot picture a room, a person, or a kind of file. Nielsen's account is that people have time to read only about a quarter of the text on the pages they actually open. The quarter they read should be the matter and the way to ask. Decoration that pushes those words below the first screen spends the only seconds you are likely to get.

A calm photograph of the real office, or of the people who take the meetings, can stay. It should be a specific room. The sentence next to it still has to do the sorting.

Watch the hero for a second failure mode. Some firms write a clear matter line, then set it in small type over a full-bleed texture, with the consultation link in a menu. The words exist. The first glance still reads as stone. If the matter and the request are not the largest readable things in the first view, the costume won.

## What belongs under that first view

Once the opening is honest, the rest of the page can support it. Keep a stable order.

1. The matter, and the request for a consultation.
2. Two or three matter types, each with a boundary.
3. Who does that work, by name and role, with a link to the people behind it.
4. One proof point you can publish: a kind of client, a type of work you are allowed to describe, a constraint you are known for handling. Check the rules of your jurisdiction before you publish an outcome.
5. A short note on how a consultation works, including what to have ready.
6. The request again, for the person who scrolled.

Each block should add a fact the first screen did not say. A second marble banner does not add a fact. A paragraph that restates "excellence" does not add a fact.

Google's people-first questions are a useful edit. Would someone who came to you directly learn enough to decide whether to request time? Is it plain who stands behind the page? Trust is the part of experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trust that Google treats as the most important. On a homepage, trust is a named matter and a named next step.

## How to review the first ten seconds

You can review this page in an afternoon, without a research panel.

Open the live page on a phone. Hand it to someone who did not write the copy and who knows what it is like to be short on time. Give them about ten seconds. Hide the page. Ask two questions. What kinds of matters does this practice take? How would you request a consultation?

If they describe a mood, the matter line is still missing or still too quiet. If they know the matter and cannot say how to ask, the action is vague or easy to miss. Change those two things before you add a section lower down.

Then read the first screen out loud, without the layout. Jakob Nielsen's practical rule, in that same Nielsen Norman Group article, is that a page has to communicate its value within 10 seconds if it wants several minutes of attention. For this site, the value is a matter you take and a way to ask for time. If you need the marble to make the firm feel serious, the words are not finished.

Run the test with one real matter in mind. Ask a colleague to pretend they have a commercial lease that renews in three weeks. If they cannot tell whether you want that work, the homepage is still a general brochure.

## When the practice really is broad

Some firms take many kinds of matters, and pretending otherwise would be false. The homepage can still sort. "Business matters for owner-led companies" is a kind. The services page can split leases, employment, and contracts. The homepage does not have to pretend the split is invisible, and it does not have to list every split in the hero.

Formal tone is allowed. Formal is short sentences, a clear name, and a real room. It does not require Latin, and it does not require hiding the consultation under a menu called Inquiries.

If the first screen is doing this job, the next page a client opens is often the one about money. They want to know whether the shape of the fee fits the matter before they write a long email. Read [how a pricing page lets a client judge fit](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-law-practice) before you publish a fee section that only says to get in touch.

When you want that first screen compared with other sites that had to be specific, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful question is whether a stranger can see the offer without a tour.
